Games with creative mechanics that are born from limitations are often some of my favorite games. Games that trade player control away in return for simplicity, on the other hand, are often some of my most [b]hated[/b] games.

Rare is the game that better demonstrates the distinction between those two categories than [b]Kingdom[/b].

You'd be forgiven for thinking [b]Kingdom[/b] started off as a mobile game, because it makes one of the most common critical mistakes made by mobile games throughout the early to mid 2010s--the very mistake, in fact, that gave rise to the initial wave of hatred around early mobile games once big-name publishers started releasing mobile cash grabs wearing the skinsuits of their popular franchises. And no, it had nothing to do with mobile monetization, at least not initially.

It had to do with the way the mobile entries had to pare down the gameplay of the originals due to platform limitations. The controls and mechanics were simplified, not in a way that streamlined the games and made them feel more pleasant to play, but in ways that replaced player control or agency with the game simply [i]doing those things for you[/i]--the logical end of this being Korean autoplay MMO grinders, but it started off less nefarious, though no less annoying.

The bottom line of my rambling is that instead of treating hardware limitations as an opportunity to develop creative new mechanics that were equally fun as the originals, these early mobile games would almost always just dumb down the original style of gameplay by just automating the parts they couldn't make work well with mobile controls, and tried to pass it off as "just like the original game, but in your pocket!" And nobody was fooled, for the most part.

[b]Kingdom[/b] does [i]precisely[/i] this with the side-scrolling strategy/tower defense subgenre, but without the excuse of having been a mobile game prior to its PC release. In fact, I can't find anything about its development history that might possibly suggest why the developers did not allow the player to at least tell your troops to go to the other front, or control which kind of item a new recruit will pick up, or AT LEAST have an undo button on walls or created items to help the player recover from the game deciding to send a worker to the opposite side of the kingdom from where you need him.

But no, as the player you are only allowed to collect money and spend it--everything else is automated. You might think that sounds cool, like it'd allow you to plan several steps ahead and focus on the management level of the game, but no. You start to realize very rapidly that all the planning you're doing amounts to little more than working around the niggling annoyances the game itself is causing you with its automated portion--like not filling up the towers you built with archers immediately, or workers prioritizing running to the opposite side of the kingdom to bring a catapult over instead of upgrading the wall you just queued up, even though they'll never get the catapult over before the unbuilt wall is overrun by enemies. And that is only one example of the many, MANY annoying circumstances that can arise due to the game's automation, and many of these circumstances can be outright run-ending until you know the exact order to do things in such that the game responds in the way you want it to.

It's truly frustrating. I get that the game is free, and as a free time-waster on Kongregate (where it started off), it'd be fine enough I guess.

But [b]Kingdom[/b] is not a game for people wanting a game, with all the meat that word implies. It's a game for people wanting a time-waster, a tool to avoid having to do something they don't want to do like work or school. And those are the types of people who wrote the glowing "Very Positive" reviews on the game here, whether they're aware of it or not.

Bear that in mind, and be sure you know which category you're in, before bothering to give this game any of your time.

The main reason why I am leaving a negative review is because, despite being 'Verified' for Steam Deck, this game doesn't work at all on Steam Deck. It doesn't even load up, so I'm not sure why it's still verified.

Anyway, Kingdom was a fun and charming game back in the day despite it's flaws, but it's clear that someone at Raw Fury has continued updating the game ever since Noio (the developer) left the franchise. As such, it has turned into something different from the original game. Something about it feels off, whether it's the difficulty balancing or the procedural generation or the fact that they've added elements from the sequel that don't fit this particular game and/or don't seem to work properly.

Yes, they have fixed some of the issues from the original version of the game, but the biggest and most frustrating issue- the fact that available archers won't immediately fill empty towers when a new day starts- remained un-fixed. So ultimately, it isn't really a 'net gain' over previous versions of the game.

Kingdom was an important and influential game, but in this current state (and especially without the handheld functionality that is promised on the store page) it simply isn't worth playing anymore. It feels every bit like a Frankenstein game that was tweaked and updated without the original creators on board, and the end result feels like it has lost some of the magic and soul of the original game, just as Two Crowns (one of the sequels that was developed without Noio) failed to recapture the magic and the soul of the previous games.

If you want to experience this style of game as Noio intended, then you should either play Kingdom: New Lands (which is, and always was, the far superior game) or wait for Garbage Country (their upcoming game).

[b]🏰 Kingdom: Classic: O reinado minimalista que testa sua paciência e astúcia[/b]

Você começa sem nada, só um rei (ou rainha) a cavalo e uma bolsa de moedas. Cada moeda que você joga no chão pode significar expansão… ou desastre total. Kingdom: Classic é simples na superfície, você gasta, recruta e constrói, mas esconde uma tensão poderosa por horas.


[b]🌄 Um mundo pixelado que respira com a luz do dia… e treme à noite[/b]

A estética é impressionante para um pixel art minimalista: reflexos na água, ciclos de dia e noite cheios de atmosfera .

Durante o dia você expande, contrata construtores, faz agricultores trabalharem. À noite, surgem as ondas, os “Greedlings”, que atacam sem dó.


[b]📈 Progressão que exige olhar atento e nervos de aço[/b]

- A curva de dificuldade cresce com brutalidade: você aprende pelas mãos, na base do trial & error.
- Plantar uma fazenda demais ou esquecer uma muralha aqui dá o gosto amargo da derrota. Se os pilares (exército, tesouro) chegam ao extremo, você morre.
- Há um loop viciante: cada falha ensina algo novo, e você tenta de novo, sem tutorial explicar nada.


[b]✅ Por que Kingdom agrada (e vicia)[/b]

- [b]Pixel art magnífica[/b], que brilha tanto no amanhecer quanto na escuridão da noite.
- [b]Simplicidade estratégica[/b], o jogo faz uma torre de comando com poucas mecânicas e altíssimo potencial.
- [b]Reinícios significativos[/b], cada run é um novo aprendizado tático.
- [b]Eventos misteriosos e upgrades escondidos[/b] em criptas e ruínas próximas.


[b]❌ Onde pode decepcionar quem quer mais de um city builder[/b]

- [b]Repetição chega forte depois do dia 50[/b] 
- [b]AI dos súditos é limitada e, às vezes, frustrante[/b], eles podem se perder ou agir de forma burra.
- [b]Pouca variedade de inimigos[/b], são basicamente 3 tipos de monstros.
- [b]Sem progressão além do mapa começado[/b], quando acaba, só resta recomeçar.


[b]🌟 Conclusão: um reino onde o simples exige tanto quanto o complexo[/b]

Après un bref tutoriel, [i]Kingdom: Classic[/i] vous propulse dans la peau d'un roi/d'une reine devant établir une petite base. Sur son fidèle destrier, votre personnage va alors devoir explorer les environs pour trouver et enrôler des sujets dévoués afin de construire, étendre et défendre votre modeste royaume.

En effet, des créatures maléfiques attaqueront votre camp une fois la nuit venue et il vous incombe, dans un premier temps, de les repousser, puis, à long terme, de détruire les portails qui les génèrent. Pour survivre durablement, il vous faudra donc gérer et collecter les ressources comme l'or et le recrutement d'unités.

Malgré ce gameplay simpliste, le jeu est plutôt addictif et plaisant, même si la lassitude survient rapidement une fois que l'on a compris les mécaniques basiques pour faire beaucoup d'argent.

En revanche, j'ai regretté l'absence d'une interface montrant le nombre d'unités. Par ailleurs, l'impossibilité "d'accélérer le temps" entre les vagues est également regrettable car cette fonctionnalité aurait été bien utile pour le long défi de la survie des 100 jours. Malgré cela, l'ensemble reste globalement agréable bien que minimaliste.
